Validating a stage-acoustics engine by calibration burden

What does each decibel of accuracy cost? Seven measured reference scenes and three concert rooms, with one failure recorded rather than removed.

Henry Wang1

1Shanghai High School International Division, Shanghai, China|henry2023trp@gmail.com|Working paper

22 sections 7 figures 5 tables PRISM-WP-001

Abstract

Room-acoustics simulation is usually validated by agreement with measurements after calibration, which leaves the reader unable to tell how much of the agreement the calibration bought. We validate a geometrical-acoustics engine built for orchestral stages — image sources in a shoebox with a statistical late field, first-order Biot–Tolstoy–Medwin edge diffraction, a measured loudspeaker directivity and a finite-difference wave solver as reference — on a ladder ordered by calibration burden: from a finite reflecting plate the engine had never seen, predicted with nothing fitted under a pre-registered protocol, through single-parameter and single-calibration scenes, to a concert hall whose geometry was fitted on one measurement set and tested on another. With nothing fitted, the engine predicts the field behind a 1–2 m plate, rigid or absorbing, within 0.7 dB median and 4.7 dB at the 90th percentile over 160 Hz–8 kHz, and the reflection from a rigid plate to 1.0 dB median; it over-predicts the reflection from an absorbing plate by 8–10 dB at 1.25–4 kHz, where the rigid-edge approximation in the diffraction model is the declared suspect. A second held-out test on a slotted 3 × 3 reflector array and on two parallel plates, run under a corrected and again frozen protocol, locates the model's missing term in frequency: from 500 Hz to 8 kHz first-order diffraction from 36 edges predicts the array's reflection — and its gaps, where no specular path exists — within 0.7 dB median and 2 dB at the 90th percentile, while below 500 Hz it over-predicts by 6–9 dB, compounding with each reflection between the plates. Every other declared mechanism criterion — a floor reflection, a partition, a body, rows of seats — was missed, most of them narrowly, and the misses are reported as declared. In the Detmold Konzerthaus, calibrated only to the measured T30, it predicts clarity at one seat within 2.1 dB RMS over six octaves; with the hall's plan fitted on one measurement set and tested on another, it reproduces level patterns across 272 source–seat pairs with r = 0.67–0.86 but fails the early-to-late energy ratios at 125–500 Hz, in the same way in one calibrated pair, in 24 transfer pairs and in the fitted hall; perturbing the calibration by the just-noticeable ±5 % moves those metrics by less than half a JND, so the failure is geometric and no calibration removes it. On one machine, first-order diffraction costs 8 ms per source–receiver pair and is converged at 50 quadrature nodes; image-source order is free and buys no clarity past order 2; the wave solver reaches 0.02 Hz modal accuracy at a 4 cm grid. Two defects of the first pre-registered protocol, corrected and tested in the second, and two of the cost benchmark's fidelity axes are reported without re-scoring.

1. Introduction

Geometrical acoustics is the workhorse of room simulation, and its validation has a settled form: a measured room, a calibrated model, and a table of ISO 3382-1 parameters agreeing within a just-noticeable difference or two. The international round robins (Vorländer 1995; Bork 2000, 2005; Brinkmann et al. 2019) established that the disagreement between codes is largest exactly where the calibration cannot reach — diffraction, scattering, the low-frequency wave regime — and the BRAS benchmark (Brinkmann et al. 2019; Aspöck et al. 2021) was built to expose those mechanisms one at a time in measured reference scenes. What a validation paper still rarely states is the calibration burden of each agreement: how many measured numbers from the room under test entered the model before the comparison was made, and what the model predicts when none do.

This paper reports the validation of a propagation engine written for a different purpose — simulating what each player of a symphony orchestra hears from every other, on a real stage, for a behavioural model of ensemble timing — and organises the evidence by that burden. The organising question is not "does the engine agree" but "what does it predict with nothing fitted, what does one fitted number buy, and where does it break". The answer has both halves. With nothing fitted, the engine's first-order edge diffraction reproduces the sound field behind finite plates to within the declared criteria in a scene whose responses no analysis code had opened before the protocol was frozen; several other declared mechanism criteria were missed, most narrowly. In a real hall, the engine reproduces the spatial pattern of level and the interaural cues across 272 source–seat pairs and fails the early-energy ratios at 125–500 Hz in every form of the comparison, calibrated or transferred. The failure is the paper's most useful result, because a sensitivity test shows that no admissible calibration removes it, which locates it in the geometric early field.

Three things distinguish this validation from the usual form. The held-out scene was pre-registered: the protocol, criteria, priors and analysis code were hashed before any of its impulse responses were opened by analysis code, and the verdicts are reported as declared even where the protocol proved defective. Every metric is computed by the same code on the measured and the simulated response, so that the comparison cannot favour the model through a different estimator. And cost is reported as a first-class result, as error against wall time on one machine at increasing fidelity, so that a reader can see where the engine's next decibel would come from and what it would cost.

2. The engine and the measurements

2.1 The engine

The engine (orchestra/acoustics/shoebox.py, orchestra/world/) is an image-source model of a rectangular room (Allen & Berkley 1979) with frequency-dependent absorption per surface in octave bands 125 Hz–4 kHz, ISO 9613-1 air absorption, and the real source's measured radiation pattern evaluated for every image path toward the receiver mirrored through the same sequence of planes (exact for planar reflections). Image sources are kept up to the completeness time of the lattice, (N + 1) L_min / c for order N, and a statistical late field — Gaussian noise per band with the energy density of the image lattice, decaying with the room's per-band reverberation time — begins at that time. The reverberation time of the late field is either derived from the surfaces (Eyring; "blind" below) or set to a measured T30 per band ("calibrated"). Impulse responses are rendered with fractional (windowed-sinc) delays at any sample rate.

Two additions matter for the scenes below. Obstacles — partitions, bodies, finite plates — diffract at their edges by the first-order Biot–Tolstoy–Medwin edge-source integral (Svensson, Fred & Vanderkooy 1999; frequency-domain form Asheim & Svensson 2013), orchestra/world/diffraction.py, with Gauss–Legendre quadrature graded quadratically toward the apex point and split there. Edges are treated as rigid regardless of the face's absorption; this approximation is stated in advance and is where the engine fails in §4.1. Sources are the Genelec 8020c whose directivity BRAS measured on a 2° grid (Brinkmann et al. 2019), stored as third-octave complex spectra and interpolated in direction and frequency; below 200 Hz the pattern is omnidirectional. For the Detmold measurements, made with a Neumann KH120 for which no measured pattern is available, the Genelec pattern shifted down in frequency by the ratio of cabinet sizes (1.2) serves as a proxy (S20), and an assumed two-way-monitor rear attenuation of 0–16 dB per octave band serves in S7–S7c; both are assumptions, not measurements.

A finite-difference time-domain solver (orchestra/acoustics/fdtd.py: standard leapfrog, second order, node-centred, locally reacting impedance boundaries with a ghost node and a backward time difference) provides a wave-based reference below the Schroeder frequency, where the geometrical model cannot represent modes or interference.

2.2 The measurements

  • BRAS reference scenes (Brinkmann et al. 2019; Aspöck et al. 2021; CC BY 4.0): RS1, a single

reflection off the tiled floor of a hemi-anechoic chamber (ten pairs); RS2, a square plate of 25 mm MDF, 1 m or 2 m, bare or faced with Rockfon SONAR-G, in a fully anechoic chamber (54 pairs); RS5, a 2.07 m partition (11 shadow pairs); RS6, a 0.72 × 0.72 × 4.14 m body (9 pairs); RS7, fifteen bars of 0.24 m height at 0.34 m pitch (8 pairs). Responses in pascal; positions to the millimetre; the loudspeaker calibrated to 80 dB SPL at 1 kHz, 2 m on axis.

  • Detmold SRIR (Amengual Garí et al. 2020; Zenodo 4116247): the Konzerthaus Detmold (V ≈ 4600 m³), Set A, one loudspeaker on

stage, one stage receiver 0.62 m behind it and one seat; Set B, eight loudspeakers on stage and three audience receivers (24 pairs); Set C, an 8-loudspeaker grid on stage measured at a grid of seats with an omnidirectional, a figure-of-eight and a KU 100 head (272 source–receiver pairs; 264 for G, which is taken relative to the nearest seat); and Set A of two further rooms, the Brahmssaal (a rectangular chamber hall with an apse, 8.1 × 18.3 m) and the Sommertheater (a proscenium theatre, 14.9 × 28 m, with a stage house and balconies).

Room metrics (T30, EDT, C80, D50, centre time, early and late support, G, JLF, ILD, ITD, IACC) are computed with one implementation (orchestra/acoustics/room_metrics.py) on both sides of every comparison. Just-noticeable differences are ISO 3382-1 Table A.1 (EDT and T30 5 %, C80 1 dB, D50 0.05, Ts 10 ms, G 1 dB), support 1 dB by analogy with G (declared), JLF 0.05, ILD 2 dB, ITD 50 µs, IACC 0.075. A comparison "agrees" when its RMS error over pairs is within one JND, is "approximate" within two, and "fails" beyond (protocol docs/04, frozen 2026-09-14).

3. Is the solver right where the answer is known?

Before any measurement, the engine was checked against cases with analytic answers (12_numerical_verification.json). Rendered level follows 1/r within 0.013 dB out to 32 m with zero delay error; two coherent sources reproduce the analytic interference to 0.008 dB RMS, with the null at −25.39 dB against −25.34 dB exact; one source over a rigid plane gives both arrival times to 10⁻¹² s and the comb filter to 0.043 dB RMS; four isolated modes of a 5 × 4 × 3 m hard box are reproduced by the image lattice to 1.29 Hz at worst; rendered energy equals the sum of path energies within 0.009 dB, decreases monotonically with absorption, and no path exceeds its free-field gain. The engine's seated-player insertion-loss model (Porcinai & Weinzierl 2025) sits 1.4–4.2 dB below the barrier law of Maekawa (1968) on the same knife-edge geometry, which is the first sign, later confirmed on RS5–RS6, that it under-attenuates. Convergence with image-source order is monotone (last step 0.50 dB in the pair energy; the seed of the late field moves the band levels by 0.066 dB SD).

The wave solver was checked against the analytic modes of a hard box (13_wave_reference.json). Its declared convergence curve was not monotone, and the reason is recorded rather than smoothed over: the solver snaps the box to whole cells, so at every grid step but 0.10 m it simulates a box 0.6–1.8 % off 2.0 × 1.7 × 1.4 m, and modal frequencies scale with dimension. Scored against the modes of the box actually simulated (a post-hoc correction, reproduced by 51_engine_paper_figures.py and reported with the benchmark in §6), the RMS modal error falls monotonically from 0.095 Hz at 0.10 m to 0.019 Hz at 0.04 m. On a shared 2.0 × 1.7 × 1.4 m room with α = 0.1 the geometrical and wave models agree to 2.4 dB RMS in third octaves between 40 and 400 Hz (bias −0.08 dB; narrowband correlation 0.94), and on a stage-sized 8 × 6 × 5 m box with α = 0.15 to 1.16 dB RMS up to 300 Hz (bias +0.77 dB), which bounds what the geometrical model loses by ignoring the wave regime in a room of that size.

4. Nothing fitted: the reference scenes

4.1 RS2, the held-out plate (pre-registered)

The protocol (docs/15_engine_validation_preregistration.md) fixed the geometry from the BRAS documentation, two models — specular-only (the engine's image-source logic on a finite plate) and specular + BTM (the same plus first-order edge diffraction from the four edges, 300 quadrature nodes; primary) — two observables, and the criteria, before any RS2 response was opened by analysis code (hash docs/PREREG_48.json). Reflection-side pairs (36): the plate's contribution isolated in a window from 1 ms before the geometric image-path time to 12 ms after, in third-octave bands 160 Hz–8 kHz, against the predicted plate contribution; criteria median |error| ≤ 2.5 dB, 90th percentile ≤ 6 dB, arrival within 0.3 ms in every pair. Shadow-side pairs (18): the total level in a 40 ms window, criteria median ≤ 3 dB, p90 ≤ 8 dB. Cells where a model predicts nothing are scored at −40 dB re free field. Nothing was fitted; the declared priors for the full primary criterion were 0.6 (rigid) and 0.45 (absorbing).

Three results and two defects follow.

The shadow passes. Behind the plate the primary model is within 0.72 dB median and 4.7 dB p90 on the rigid plates and 0.48 / 1.67 dB on the absorbing one, with nothing fitted, across 160 Hz–8 kHz. Specular-only is 11–24 dB off there because it predicts nothing. This is pure first-order diffraction from four thin edges, and it is the cleanest positive result in the paper.

The rigid reflection is right in level and time. Over all 324 rigid cells the primary model is within 1.02 dB median and 3.32 dB p90, inside the declared thresholds, and wherever a specular reflection exists (20 on-plate pairs) it arrives within 0.11 ms of the image-path time. The class nevertheless fails as declared, through the arrival criterion, for a reason that is a defect of the protocol, not of the model: the protocol asserted that "the direct sound arrives ≥ 8 ms earlier in every pair". It does not — the image-minus-direct gap is 3.1–11.7 ms and 24 of the 36 pairs are below 8 ms — so the reflection window opens 3.5–7.8 ms after the direct sound's peak, inside the loudspeaker's own decay (−32 to −55 dB re its peak). Where the plate contributes only edge diffraction (16 pairs whose specular point lies off the plate, 14–28 dB below the direct sound), that residual sits 7–34 dB below the window's peak, exceeds the detector's threshold within the first 0.2 ms, and the "arrival" is the window's first sample. The criterion "in every pair" was undefined for those pairs as measured. Split post hoc by whether the specular point lies on the plate (Table 2), the uncontaminated rigid pairs meet every declared threshold (0.74 dB median, 2.77 dB p90, 10 of 10 arrivals within 0.3 ms); the off-plate rigid agreement (1.32 dB) is agreement with a contaminated observable and is not evidence for the edge model — the shadow class is.

The absorbing reflection is over-predicted, and the reason was declared in advance. On the absorbing plates the error is a bias of +3.5 dB concentrated at 1.25–4 kHz, where Rockfon SONAR-G absorbs most: +8 to +10.5 dB per band on the 1 m plate and +4 to +7 dB on the 2 m plate. On the centre pair of the 1 m plate the measured plate contribution across 1.25–3.15 kHz is −4.6 to +0.3 dB re free field; specular-only predicts −7.2 to −3.6 dB, specular + BTM +1.4 to +5.0 dB, and the same pair on the rigid plate is matched within 0.3 dB in every one of those bands. The protocol's one declared approximation — edges rigid on both surfaces — predicts exactly this: on the rigid plate the edges are a small correction to a strong specular reflection; on the absorbing plate the specular reflection is 10–20 dB down and the unattenuated edges dominate the prediction. That the measurement lies between the two models on every absorbing on-plate pair is consistent with the diagnosis and does not prove it; an absorbing-wedge diffraction model is the test.

4.2 RS1 and the mechanism scenes RS5–RS7

These were the engine's first measured tests (protocol docs/04, criteria declared before each run; 18_p1_rs1.json, 18b_diffraction_scenes.json; Fig. 5). All of them were missed, and the record is reported as it stands.

RS1, one reflection off a floor. Criterion: third-octave RMS ≤ 1 dB over the ten pairs and comb-filter notches within 1/24 octave. With the documented geometry the median RMS is 1.96 dB (worst pair 3.04) and 42 % of notches are within criterion. Fitting one number — the height of the reflecting datum, 0.099 m above the documented floor, from the arrival times (tier 1) — brings the median to 1.05 dB (worst 1.93), and adding the loudspeaker's measured phase to 1.09 dB (worst 1.43) with 62 % of notches in criterion. The criterion is 1 dB: a narrow miss, twice. The diagnosed causes are the datum offset and the direction-dependent acoustic centre of a two-way loudspeaker. The datum did not transfer: applied unchanged to RS5–RS7 it made every model worse, so it is a calibration of RS1, not a property of the chamber.

RS5, a 2.07 m partition (11 shadow pairs, criterion RMS ≤ 2 dB). The engine's seated-player insertion loss, a knife-edge formula, gives 5.55 dB median RMS (max 6.99). First-order BTM at the partition's top edge gives 2.28 dB median (max 4.12): a narrow miss that halves the engine's error.

RS6, a 0.72 × 0.72 × 4.14 m body (9 pairs, ≤ 3 dB). Engine 8.09 dB median (max 9.49); BTM on an equivalent thin screen at the Bullington edge 3.54 dB (max 4.60). A thick body needs the second-order term, which is implemented but fails its thin-limit test and is not used.

RS7, fifteen bars — the seat-dip effect (Schultz & Watters 1964; 8 pairs; dip within 1/3 octave and 3 dB; band RMS ≤ 3 dB, 63 Hz–1 kHz). The engine has no model for rows and is 9.62 dB median off with the dip 13–21 dB too shallow. A quarter-wave "seat plane" model (locally reacting wells between the bars) places the dip within 1/3 octave in 3 of 4 pairs in its domain and within 3 dB in 2 of 4, but its band RMS is 8.6 dB median. The dip's frequency is captured; its broadband level is not, and a wave-based treatment is the stated next step.

Read together with RS2: first-order edge diffraction is the engine's most accurate physical mechanism when the edge is thin and rigid (RS2 shadow, pass; RS5, 2.3 dB), and the engine's remaining mechanism errors are thick bodies (RS6), absorbing edges (RS2 absorbing face) and grazing propagation over rows (RS7).

4.3 RS3 and RS4: the second held-out test, with the corrected protocol (pre-registered)

The two defects of §4.1 were corrected in a second protocol (docs/17, frozen with S52 as docs/PREREG_52.json before any RS3 or RS4 response was opened): reflection windows [t_k − 1 ms, t_k + 12 ms] defined from the geometry; a scorability gate decided from the measurement alone — a window counts only if the RMS level of the millisecond before t_k is at least 10 dB below that of the 3 ms from t_k — with the number of excluded windows an outcome; the arrival criterion on scorable windows only; and a direct-sound window [t_d − 1, t_d + 4 ms] as a secondary test of calibration and directivity. Models, criteria and thresholds as in §4.1; diffraction with 100 quadrature nodes (§6); air absorption by ISO 9613-1 from the documented temperature and humidity. RS3: two rigid 2 m plates 10 m apart, one on-axis pair, image chains to order 4 with first-order diffraction of every image (at most three bounces), six windows at 10, 16, 24, 30, 36 and 44 m. RS4: nine rigid 0.68 m plates in a 3 × 3 array with 0.13 m gaps, 36 edges; nine "on-centre" pairs aimed at the centre plate and nine "off-centre" pairs aimed at the gap between rows (all nine of the latter turn out to be diffraction-only: no specular point falls on a plate). Priors were 0.7 (RS4 on-centre), 0.5 (off-centre), 0.5 (RS3 order 1), 0.35 (orders 2–4), 0.5 (direct).

Specular-only fails every class but RS3 order 1 (where it also passes, 2.23 / 5.24 dB) and predicts nothing in the off-centre windows (34 dB median error).

The gate did its work. Six of 24 windows were excluded — the three RS4 pairs with the shortest direct-to-image gap and no specular path (margins 5.9–9.5 dB) and RS3's three weakest orders (4.0–6.3 dB) — and every one of them shows the RS2 artefact of an "arrival" at the window's first sample; no scorable window does. Where the criterion applies, arrivals are within 0.13 ms in RS4 and 0.04 ms at RS3's first order; the two scorable higher orders of RS3 arrive 0.63 and 0.39 ms early (0.22 and 0.13 m), which a single plate-position error does not explain and which is reported as the miss it is.

Every level failure is below 500 Hz. Split post hoc by band, the primary model on RS4 is within 0.72 / 2.14 dB (median / p90) on-centre and 0.54 / 1.73 dB off-centre from 500 Hz to 8 kHz — the off-centre class being pure first-order diffraction from 36 edges with no specular path at all — and over-predicts by +5.9 and +6.2 dB mean (per band +8.9, +8.6, +5.9, +3.8 dB) at 160–400 Hz. In RS3 the over-prediction grows with every bounce: +12 dB at 160 Hz after two reflections, +27 dB after four, while from 500 Hz up the scorable higher orders stay within 1.7 dB median. The prior's reasoning had the direction wrong: it expected trouble above 2.6 kHz, where the gap exceeds a wavelength. The failure is where the gap — and in RS3 the plate — is smaller than the wavelength. There the first-order contributions of the two edges bounding a narrow slot do not cancel as the true field does, and a plate one wavelength wide reflects far less than its image source; both are the edge-to-edge (second-order) term the model declares it lacks. RS2's absorbing face pointed at the same term from another side. Its absence is now located in frequency. Gating the prediction with the measurement's window (post hoc) changes the predicted levels by at most 0.9 dB at 160 Hz, so the observable's asymmetry is not the cause.

The direct window is within 0.3–0.6 dB median everywhere; the on-centre p90 misses by 0.12 dB through a +2 to +4 dB over-prediction at 5–8 kHz on every pair (the interpolated pattern at 60–90° off axis) and +1.8 dB at 160 Hz (the pattern is omnidirectional below 200 Hz by BRAS's construction).

5. One calibrated number, then transfer, then a fitted hall

5.1 Tier 2: the Konzerthaus with its measured T30

With the measured T30 per band setting the late decay and everything else predicted (07_detmold_validation.json, monitor-directivity variant; Fig. 6a): C80 at the seat is within 0.44–1.32 dB at 500 Hz–4 kHz and off by +4.1 and +2.6 dB at 125 and 250 Hz; early support at the stage receiver is within 0.1–1.3 dB at 125 Hz–1 kHz and −3.4 / −3.3 dB at 2 and 4 kHz; late support is −0.8 to −3.6 dB across bands; the seat–stage level difference is within 1.8 dB in every band. The pattern that recurs at every later tier is already here: the high bands agree, the low bands of every early-to-late ratio do not.

5.2 Tier 3: transfer to 24 pairs and to two other rooms

Set B, 24 pairs (07b_detmold_setB.json; Fig. 6b): C80 RMS error 2.3–2.9 dB at 500 Hz–4 kHz and 3.5–4.6 dB at 125–250 Hz, with a positive bias of +1.1 to +3.2 dB in every band (the model is too clear); D50 RMS 0.11–0.19; centre time RMS 15–34 ms, biased −4 to −25 ms (too early); EDT RMS 0.23–0.43 s; the level difference R2 − R1 within 0.45–1.1 dB RMS at 500 Hz–4 kHz and R3 − R1 within 0.8–2.7 dB. The source-to-source level spread at 1 kHz is reproduced in magnitude (measured SD 0.60–0.94 dB, modelled 0.58–0.71 dB) but its pattern across the eight loudspeakers correlates with the measurement only at the farthest receiver (r 0.79; 0.13 and 0.29 at the others), which is the first sign that the seat-to-seat pattern of early energy is not in the model.

Two rooms the shoebox does not describe (07c_detmold_rooms.json). Both were modelled as plain shoeboxes with the apse, stage house, balconies and curtains left out, as a challenge, with two variants: calibrated (measured T30) and blind (Eyring decay from assumed absorption). In the Brahmssaal, C80 RMS is 2.0–3.7 dB calibrated and 1.4–2.8 dB blind — the blind variant is better, because the assumed absorption happens to give a T30 within 0.16–0.47 s of the measurement and the calibrated late field is not the limiting error. In the Sommertheater the blind Eyring decay is 1.9–2.5 s against a measured 0.9–1.3 s — the stage house and curtains absorb what the shoebox has not got — and C80 is 3.1–4.4 dB RMS blind against 2.0–5.1 dB calibrated, with the calibrated model too clear by +1.9 to +3.1 dB in every band. Stage support is under-predicted in both rooms (Brahmssaal early −2.1 to −4.9 dB, late −3.9 to −6.7 dB; Sommertheater early −4.1 to +2.1, late −5.9 to +0.2). A plain shoebox transfers its clarity to within 2–5 dB and its stage support to within 2–7 dB in rooms whose shape it does not represent; where its own decay is wrong by a factor of two, the one calibrated number repairs the decay but not the early field.

5.3 Tier 4: the Konzerthaus as a fitted world, tested on 272 pairs

The hall's plan was traced from the Set A drawing, its stage height, ceiling levels, loudspeaker rows and audience rake fitted to Set A direct-sound arrival times (S19), and the world was then run on the Set C grid — eight loudspeakers, the seat grid, three receiver types — with the late decay calibrated to Set C's own T30 and the KH120 pattern proxied (S20). The comparison (20b_konzerthaus_summary_setc.json, 272 pairs, classes as in §2.2) is in Table 4 and Fig. 6c and d.

The world gets the geometry right — where the sound comes from and how loud it is at each seat: level patterns to 0.6–0.9 dB RMS at 500 Hz–4 kHz with r up to 0.86, interaural level differences with r 0.86–0.89, the direct-sound ITD with r 0.89 — and gets every early-to-late energy ratio wrong at 125–500 Hz, with seat-to-seat patterns that do not correlate with the measurement at any band. S20c tested one candidate cause, the statistical late field starting too early: raising the image order from 2 to 4 (geometric to 78 ms) reduces the C80 error at 250–500 Hz from 2.6–2.8 to 2.0–2.1 dB RMS and leaves 125 Hz and every spatial pattern where they were. A quarter to a third of the timing error is the late field's early start; the rest is not.

5.4 What the calibration buys: T30 perturbed by its JND

If the tier-2–4 agreement were bought by the T30 calibration, perturbing the calibration by a plausible amount would move the agreeing metrics by more than their JND. S49 reran the tier-2 pipeline with the measured T30 scaled by 1 ± 0.05 (the ISO 3382-1 JND, taken as the calibration uncertainty because the dataset states none) and 1 ± 0.10 (49_detmold_t30_sensitivity.json, Fig. 3).

Under ±5 %, C80 moves by 0.39–0.50 dB (JND 1 dB), D50 by ≤ 0.016 (0.05), centre time by 3.8–6.0 ms (10 ms), late support by 0.12–0.42 dB and the level difference by ≤ 0.14 dB (1 dB): all insensitive, and all below the spread of the same metric across the 24 Set B positions where that spread exists. EDT moves by 0.10–0.12 s at 250 Hz–4 kHz against a JND of 0.05–0.07 s, and T30 by 0.07–0.09 s, its own JND: both calibration-dependent, as the calibrated quantity and the one closest to it should be. Early support at the stage receiver moves by exactly zero, because with image-source order 4 the statistical tail begins at the lattice's completeness time, 118.9 ms, after the 20–100 ms early window and after the 80 ms boundary of C80 at the seat (direct sound at 32.5 ms, tail from 86 ms). Under ±10 % only C80 at 4 kHz (1.03 dB) and centre time at 250–500 Hz (11–12 ms) cross their JNDs.

The reading is symmetric. The agreements in clarity, definition, centre time, support and level are not bought by the calibration — a 5 % error in T30 moves them by less than half a JND. And the disagreements cannot be repaired by it: the early-support error of 3.3–3.4 dB at 2–4 kHz and the C80 error of +4.1 and +2.6 dB at 125–250 Hz are properties of the geometric early field that no value of T30 within ±10 % touches. The Konzerthaus failure of §5.3 is the same failure, and it is in the geometry — the missing surface scattering (every early reflection is a specular point arrival), the typical absorption values, and the shoebox's flat audience area — not in the calibration.

6. Cost per unit of accuracy

Existing runtimes come from unrelated workloads. S50 measured error against wall time on one machine (Apple M4, 10 cores, macOS 26.6, Python 3.14.3, NumPy 2.5.2, SciPy 1.18.1; one process; perf_counter median of five after a warm-up; 50_cost_benchmark.json, Fig. 4) for three scenes at increasing fidelity, each with one fixed error measure declared in advance. No criterion was declared; two of the three fidelity axes turned out to be badly chosen, and they are reported as such.

RS2, BTM quadrature nodes. Specular-only costs 0.3 ms per source–receiver pair for 720 frequencies; first-order diffraction from four edges costs 8.3 ms at 50 nodes, 36 ms at 100, 49 ms at 300 (the engine's default) and 366 ms at 1000. The median error over the 45 reflection pairs is 7.16 dB for specular-only and 1.63 dB at every BTM level — identical to thirteen significant figures, because every declared level sits on the quadrature's converged plateau. The knee is below the lowest declared level: 10 nodes is off by up to 23 dB, 25 nodes within 0.07 dB, 50 nodes within 3 × 10⁻¹¹ dB of 1000 (post hoc, reproduced by S51). The usable result is the price of the default: 300 nodes cost 6× what 50 do and buy nothing measurable.

Konzerthaus, image-source order. Wall time is 0.23 s per scene at every order from 0 to 6: in this shoebox the cost is the 3 s impulse-response synthesis at 48 kHz, the late tail and the octave filtering, and enumerating up to 13³ images is free beside it. The error is not monotone: C80 at the seat is best at order 2 (1.92 dB RMS; 2.09 at order 4, 2.15 at order 6) while early support on stage improves to order 4 (3.51 → 2.07 dB) and saturates. Order is free, and it does not buy the missing decibels.

Wave solver, grid step. 0.35 s at 0.10 m to 20.0 s at 0.03 m (time ∝ dx⁻³·⁴ over this range); the declared modal error (0.10, 1.88, 1.69, 0.64, 0.86 Hz) measures the grid's snapping of the box (§3), and the corrected error (0.095, 0.056, 0.061, 0.019, 0.021 Hz) converges monotonically to one part in 10⁴ of the modal frequencies at 0.04 m.

What the benchmark establishes: on this hardware first-order diffraction costs about thirty times a specular path and is converged at 50 nodes; image-source order is free in the shoebox model and does not improve clarity past order 2 or stage support past order 4; the wave solver's accuracy at these grid steps is limited by the grid's rendering of the geometry, not by dispersion, at a cost of seconds for a small room and minutes for a stage-sized box. The engine's next decibel in the hall will not come from more image sources, more quadrature or a finer grid; it will come from a mechanism it does not have.

7. Discussion

What the engine is good for. With nothing fitted it predicts who hears what behind an obstacle, the reflection from a slotted reflector array and from its gaps from 500 Hz to 8 kHz, and the level of a specular reflection from a rigid finite surface within the declared level thresholds, with its arrival to 0.11 ms wherever a specular reflection exists. In a real hall with one calibrated number it predicts the pattern of level, interaural level difference and direct-sound ITD across 272 source–seat pairs, which is the information a model of "who hears whom, when, and how loud" needs. Those are the claims the orchestra application rests on, and the ladder supports them.

Where it breaks, and why that is the useful result. Every early-to-late energy ratio at 125–500 Hz is wrong in every form of the hall comparison — one pair, 24 pairs, 272 pairs, three rooms — and the sensitivity test shows the calibration cannot be blamed. The early field of a shoebox with specular reflections off typical materials and a flat audience plane is not the early field of a concert hall; the seat-dip scene (RS7) and the absorbing-plate scene (RS2) show two of the missing mechanisms directly. Reporting the failure with its sensitivity analysis is what turns it from a defect into a specification for the next model: surface scattering, a second-order (edge-to-edge) diffraction term — which RS3/RS4 locate below 500 Hz for gaps and plates smaller than a wavelength, and which the absorbing face of RS2 points to as well — and a wave-based treatment of grazing propagation over rows.

Two defects of the protocol. The pre-registered RS2 protocol asserted a ≥ 8 ms direct-to-image gap that holds for 12 of 36 pairs, and declared an arrival criterion that has no meaning where there is no specular arrival. Both are recorded, neither was re-scored, and both were corrected and tested in the second pre-registered protocol (§4.3): a gate decided from the measurement alone excluded exactly the windows where the observable is undefined, and the arrival criterion was then met wherever it applied. The cost benchmark likewise declared its RS2 fidelity levels on the converged plateau and confounded its wave error with grid snapping. A pre-registered protocol does not prevent such mistakes; it makes them visible and prevents their quiet repair.

Limits. The BRAS chamber, three Detmold rooms and a hemi-anechoic floor are the whole evidence; nothing here bounds the engine in a hall of a different type. The KH120's directivity is a proxy at every Detmold tier, and the S7–S7c monitor pattern an assumption; the tier-4 geometry is fitted on Set A and its late decay on the test set's own T30, so tier 4 is a held-out test of geometry only. The Detmold plans are read from drawings at ±0.5 m. No auralisation has been tested against listeners, and nothing here says how musicians behave.

8. What this paper does not claim

It does not claim the engine predicts how musicians behave; that layer was tested separately and its predictions were found to depend on unvalidated hearing-front-end choices. It does not claim perceptual validation of any rendering. It does not claim generality beyond the room types measured. It does not claim that the diagnosis of the absorbing-plate failure (rigid edges) is established: it is consistent with the data and is the declared suspect, and the absorbing-wedge model is the test. It does not claim that a second-order diffraction term would repair the low-frequency failures of RS3 and RS4: that term is the declared missing mechanism and the frequency range is now known, but building it and re-testing on the same scenes would no longer be a held-out test.

Ethics

No participants were recruited for this work. It analyses previously measured and published acoustic datasets.

Data and code availability

The measured reference scenes derive from the BRAS database and the Detmold dataset of Amengual Garí et al. (2020), both published under CC BY 4.0. The analysis scripts and stored results referenced throughout live in the author's working repository and are not yet deposited in a public archive with a DOI; that deposit is outstanding, and until it exists the numbers here cannot be independently recomputed.

Use of artificial intelligence

The drafting, the analysis code and the figure code were produced with an AI assistant working under the author's direction. The author designed the studies, set the protocols, and is responsible for the content. The assistant is not an author.

Outstanding before submission

Six references are marked † as cited for a single standard result without having been read in full; these require checking or rephrasing. The paper has not had a critical read by anyone other than the author, and no target venue has been chosen.
